## Possible directions to investigate

Not sure it's a test issue or etcdserver issue.

I see that after key "key26" being removed, there were several compaction operations.

- The watch response of rev 3 on "key26" isn't correct.
  - The test side just records whatever responded by the etcdserver, it seems unlikely the client side (test) issue. But please double check anyway.
  - For the etcdserver side, not sure whether it's related to https://github.com/etcd-io/etcd/pull/18274. Will the deletion + compactions cause temporary revision issue? need investigation.
  - since all the data look good, so I think after rebooting all members everything will be running well. It might worth double check.

 After https://github.com/etcd-io/etcd/pull/18274 got merged, the tombstone won't be removed, but somehow I did not see the key26 in db file anymore. We need to get this sorted out.

So there are 4 items to double check/investigate. Contributions is welcome!

comments.body: Yes, you can definitely trust the time and order of the logs! For more context around the faults we're seeing: 1. `fault_injector {fault:{name:pause,type:node}}` does docker pause container, waits ~2 seconds, docker unpause container. The logs will tell you when the pause starts and when the pause ends. 2. `fault_injector {fault:{affected_nodes:[ALL],details:{asymmetric:false,disruption_type:Slowed},name:partition,type:network}}` is a network partition. It'll divide the containers into groups, and fault the connection between containers that communicate from different groups. There are different types of partitions, in this case, the disruption type is slowed, which means we slow the speed of the packets by a certain amount of ms (this is usually of the order of 100s of ms). 3. `fault_injector {fault:{details:{disruption_type:Jammed},name:clog,type:network}}` is another network fault. It'll select 1 network link between 2 containers and "jam" the connection. This means that there will be a throughput rate limit on the packets going between the 2 containers. 4. `fault_injector {fault:{affected_nodes:[client],name:throttle,type:node}}` is a container fault that limits the cpu usage of the container. It does a docker update --cpu-quota to set the limit. This usually limits it by ~50% @reporter 880 failed linearization examples could be a bit misleading here. If you go to [this search and view the map](https://linuxfoundation.antithesis.com/search?&report_name=&get_logs=false&get_logs_event_desc=), you'll notice that all the 880 failed examples, "branch off" from one history. This means that they all share the same root state. It also looks like they share *most* of the history. Our "fuzzer" does this because its trying to explore different paths. So, my guess is that we actually only found the linearization bug 1 time. And then we decided to run new timelines from states around when the bug happens, which causes us to reproduce it 879 other times. I also did some calculations for the "findability of the bug". If you ran 4x 12 hour tests, and did not see the linearization bug, statistically you could be ~99% sure the bug has been resolved. cc: @reporter @nwnt

@reporter I'm a bit confused why it would be necessary to check for leadership change before acting on a `ReadState`. The raft documentation for `ReadStates` doesn't seem to mention this caveat:
https://github.com/etcd-io/raft/blob/4f13735b20be5421ee0ff7dde7cb8b8330880576/node.go#L68-L71
(I don't know the context behind it, but I interpreted https://github.com/etcd-io/etcd/commit/e5c2dff3467e7ffead0c4c4c29b6903e6b23809a as a performance optimization to retry immediately when leadership changes to avoid waiting for the inevitable timeout.)

Is there some (undocumented?) subtlety in the raft implementation that forces etcd to check for leadership changes? Looking at the raft code, I can't quite piece together how leadership change could result in an invalid read index; whenever a node becomes a leader, it resets its `readOnly` struct, so it seems like there's no way for `ReadIndex` requests from previous terms to be mistakenly fulfilled by future terms.

If raft indeed requires its users check for leadership change before acting on `ReadStates`, the following might also be a problem in etcd: `s.leaderChanged.Notify()` is triggered when etcd gets a `Ready` with a different leader id in `SoftState` than what it saw in the last `Ready`.
https://github.com/etcd-io/etcd/blob/9f83a29b3b654efbe72078613ea839164f536a21/server/etcdserver/raft.go#L186
But, I think it's possible that leadership has changed back and forth since the last `Ready`. In that case, leadership would have changed, but the `leaderChanged` channel would remain open, and invalid `ReadState`s could be accepted by `requestCurrentIndex`. It would be safer to check if the latest term number in `Ready` is higher than the previous term number.

I don't have access to the latest antithesis logs you linked, but does this seem like a possible explanation for what they show (e.g. is it still a stale readIndex)? Since I don't know what raft executions could yield an invalid `ReadState` (even in the presence of leadership change), I don't know how to write a test case for my hypothesis yet.

@participant1  Just to better document the original problem: I don't think that's a buggy execution. It should be safe to use the "cached" commitIndex, because that commitIndex was still chosen after the `requestID` key was created, which should be enough to ensure linearizability. Raft just needs to ensure that the returned `readIndex` was up-to-date in the past when `requestID` was created. 

The simplest buggy etcd execution I can think of involves having at least two `requestID`s for ReadIndex, because the bug involves the `readOnly` queue:
- A client invokes a Range request on a follower node. The follower chooses `requestID/ctx` equal to `A` via its `linearizableReadLoop`. Because of retries, it sends `ReadIndex(ctx=A)` requests twice to the current leader, which we can call `leader1`.
- The first `ReadIndex(ctx=A)` request arrives on `leader1`. After sending and receiving heartbeats, `leader1` returns a valid `ReadIndex` gets returned for `A`; but, because of network unreliability (and duplicate sends in raft), the network still has in-flight `HeartbeatResp(ctx=A)` messages from its followers.
  + Currently, the set of messages `{ReadIndex(ctx=A); HeartbeatResp(ctx=A, from=followers)}` are in flight in the network, and will stay there for a while. **The problem will be that these messages will cause leader1 to flush ALL entries in the readOnly queue when they get received in the future.**
- `leader1` becomes disconnected from the other servers, and the other servers elect a new leader. The new leader and its follower(s) commit new entries and update etcd state.
- Next, a client invokes a new Range request. Under linearizability, this range request must see all the changes made by the new leader. The client sends this request to the now-stale `leader1`. The details of the `readOnly` queue that were omitted so far will now be important.
- For this new Range request, `leader1`'s `linearizableReadLoop` chooses `requestId=B` and calls `readOnly.addRequest(...)`. This results in `readOnly.readIndexQueue = [B]`. The heartbeat requests for `B` will not be relevant. https://github.com/etcd-io/raft/blob/4f13735b20be5421ee0ff7dde7cb8b8330880576/read_only.go#L62
- `leader1` receives `ReadIndex(ctx=A)` from the network. It calls `raft.addRequest`, resulting in `readOnly.readIndexQueue = [B; A]`.
- `leader1`'s raft receives all the `HeartbeatResp(ctx=A)`'s, which results in it calling `readOnly.advance(ctx=A)`. This causes `leader1`'s raft to return the entire list `[B; A]` as a set of validated ReadIndexes. This will result in leader1 fulfilling request `B`, despite not having the latest state, thus violating linearizability. https://github.com/etcd-io/raft/blob/4f13735b20be5421ee0ff7dde7cb8b8330880576/read_only.go#L90-L102

I think this is a bug worth fixing in the generic `raft` code, as this problem could appear in users of `raft` that choose to build on UDP (or some other unreliable network transport), which might duplicate packets even it the code avoids it. Does it make sense to make a fix there?
